Q: Batch Script on CMD to get COM port on a variable A:

Update: This is the more short version for to get only the N part from COM3

@echo off && setlocal enabledelayedexpansion 
for /f "tokens=2delims=COM:" %%i in ('mode ^| findstr /RC:"\C\O\M[0-9*]"') do set "_com=%%i" & echo/!_com!
  • :: or ::
@echo off && setlocal enabledelayedexpansion 
for /f "tokens=2delims=COM:" %%i in ('mode^|findstr /C:"COM"')do set "_com=%%i"&echo/!_com!

:: batch result 3 ::

Obs.: For command line use: for /f "tokens=2delims=COM:" %i in ('mode^|findstr "COM"')do set "_com=%i"& call echo/%_com%

Pure batch solution...

for bat file, may suggest use chgport to do this or Reg Query

By chgport:

by using this variable: !_com_[%%L]! to get COM+n

by using this variable: %%L to get n

@echo off & setlocal enabledelayedexpansion & set "_cnt=0"
cd /d "%systemroot%" 
for /f "tokens=* delims= " %%C in ('where /r . chgport.exe') do set "_chgport=%%~fC"
for /f "delims== tokens=1,2" %%i in ('!_chgport! ^| findstr /v "#"') do set /a "_cnt+=1" && set "_com_[!_cnt!]=%%i ^= %%j"
popd & echo/COM[n]:  DEVICE[id]: & for /l %%L in (1 1 !_cnt!) do echo/!_com_[%%L]!

:: for get number only :: By using %%C**
for /l %%L in (1 1 !_cnt!) do for /f %%C in ('echo/!_com_[%%L]:COM^=!') do set "_com_N=%%C" & echo/ !_com_N! = COM%%C

:: Commandline result ::

COM[n]:  DEVICE[id]:
COM3  =  \Device\huawei_cdcacm_AcmSerial1
COM4  =  \Device\huawei_cdcacm_AcmSerial0
 3 = COM3
 4 = COM4

By Reg Query : by using this variable: !_com#! to get COM+n

by using this variable: !_com#:COM=! to get n

@echo off & setlocal enabledelayedexpansion 
set _key="HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\HARDWARE\DEVICEMAP\SERIALCOMM"
for /f "tokens=1,3 delims= " %%i in ('reg query !_key! ^| find /v "HKEY"') do (
   set "_device=%%i" & set "_com#=%%j" & echo/!_com#! !_device! )

:: for get number only :: By using !_com_N:~3! to get [n]
for /f "tokens=3 delims= " %%c in ('reg query !_key! ^| find /v "HKEY"') do set "_com_N=%c"&& echo/!_com_N:~3! = !_com_N!

:: Commandline result ::

COM4 \Device\huawei_cdcacm_AcmSerial0
COM3 \Device\huawei_cdcacm_AcmSerial1
4 = COM4
3 = COM3

Q: What does annotating a variable do in the Python REPL? A:

See this question on variable annotations.

In your example, x: int just registers 'x': int as an entry in the __annotations__ global. In other words:

>>> x: int
>>> __annotations__
{'x': <class 'int'>}

(IIRC it is not recommended to access the module-level __annotations__, because it may not exist if no annotations have been created)

The int part is evaluated immediately (see also: deferred annotations) but x is not evaluated. Whereas in your second example, x is evaluated and thus raises an exception.

Q: Hilt not generating PreferencesModule_ProvidePreferencesDataStoreFactory when injecting DataStore (NoClassDefFoundError) A:

I don't see why you would need a DataStore factory here since you do not want to access its configuration. Instead, as the official guide for DataStore explains, just place this at the top level of the file that contains your PreferencesDataSource:

// At the top level of your kotlin file:
private val Context.dataStore: DataStore<Preferences> by preferencesDataStore(USER_PREFERENCES)

(You should move USER_PREFERENCES there as well.)

You can now remove providePreferencesDataStore from the Hilt module.

The PreferencesDataSource can now directly access this new dataStore property. Since it requires a Context for that, you should povide one via the constructor:

@Singleton
class PreferencesDataSource @Inject constructor(
    @ApplicationContext context: Context,
) {
    private val dataStore = context.dataStore

    // ...
}

Each PreferencesDataSource instance will now have its own private dataStore property, but it will always refer to the same that was declared on the file level. You shouldn't have multiple instances of the same DataStore, though, so marking PreferencesDataSource with @Singleton takes care of that.

You can now also remove providePreferencesDataSource from the Hilt module.

This should take care of the issue you experienced.

Not related, but you should also improve the following:

  1. Use cases can leverage the Kotlin operator syntax to be more concise and expressive. You can replace the execute function with this:

    operator fun invoke(): Flow<UserPreferences> =
    repository.getUserPreferences()

    Instead of calling execute() on an instance of the use case, you can now directly invoke it, like this:

    getUserPreferencesUseCase().collect { ... }

    See https://developer.android.com/topic/architecture/domain-layer#use-cases-kotlin for more.

  2. You should not collect Flows in the view model. Instead, simply pass them through. If needed you can transform them on the way using the various Flow operations like map, flatMapLatest, combine and so on, but as the last operation you should convert them into StateFlows with stateIn.

    Remove everything in the body of the view model and simply replace it with this:

    val userPreferences: StateFlow<UserPreferences> = getUserPreferencesUseCase()
    .stateIn(
        scope = viewModelScope,
        started = SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5.seconds),
        initialValue = UserPreferences(),
    )

    This resulting Flow can now automatically stop the underlying Flow depending on its subscribers. The policy used here is SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5.seconds), which stops the DataStore flow when nobody is currently collecting userPreferences - which might happen when the user navigated to somewhere else or sent the app to the background. To prevent minor interruptions to stop and restart the flow, all of this happens only after a 5 second delay, so configuration changes f.e. have enough time to resubscribe to userPreferences.

Q: How to unindent in Vim without leaving Insert mode? A:

It's possible to issue a single Normal mode command from Insert mode with Ctrl-O. To de-indent with the familiar <<, press <C-O><< in Insert mode (increase indent with <C-O>>>). To apply the default indent, use <C-O>==. See :help i_CTRL-O.

This works well when you know the Normal mode indentation commands by heart but not the matching Insert mode commands Ctrl-D, Ctrl-T and Ctrl-F (see :help i_CTRL-D, :help i_CTRL-T and :help i_CTRL-F, respectively).

For easy reference, here's a table with indentation commands, their native modes and how to use each from Insert mode:

mode decrease apply increase use from Insert mode
Insert Ctrl-D Ctrl-F Ctrl-T
Normal with motion <{motion} ={motion} >{motion} prefix Ctrl-O
Normal, current line << == >> prefix Ctrl-O
Command-line :[range]< :[range]= :[range]> prefix Ctrl-O

Q: What are the pros and cons of using NULL values in SQL as opposed to default values? A:

The simplest example ever: You have a table to record the weather. Every day you create a record with the following columns: id, date, temperature, pressure, uv_level, precipitation. You have connected a meteorological device which sends those parameters every day. One day the thermometer stopped working and stopped sending temperature to the computer.

If you have temperature non-nullable with default 0, you would think the actual temperature on that day was 0C, which is incorrect.

If you make that column non-nullable with no default value, your inserted record will be failing because of having no temperature value; unless you send ZERO again, it will similarly be incorrect.

If you make that column nullable and no value is sent by the thermometer, this would suggest that something is wrong with the device, but so far (if you ever need min, max, or average temperatures) your data will be correct.

Q: Using df.styler with df.to_latex() and longtable A:

FWIW, this ended up working for me...without needing to explicitly invoke longtable.

styler = df.style
styler.format(
    precision=0, thousands=",", escape="latex")
styler.map_index(lambda v: "font-weight: bold;", axis="index")
styler.map_index(lambda v: "font-weight: bold;", axis="columns")
p = styler.to_latex(
    caption="Raw observation counts and sums of weights",
    convert_css=True,
    position_float="centering",
    multicol_align="|c|",
    hrules=True,
    )

I'm guessing maybe it had to do with how I invoked it in the Markdown document itself, which was as follows.

\centering
\input{/Users/griffinjmbur/Desktop/code/working-drafts/diss2figs/sample_sizes.tex}

Q: Compiling an application for use in highly radioactive environments A:

Interestingly nobody mentioned that compilers usually have some flags to make the final binaries more secure. Usually, those actions apply to cyber security threats, but if we use our imagination, a 'random bit flip' might be a cyber attack (null terminated strings aren't null terminated anymore).

It was tagged with gcc, so here is a relevant answer how to make a binary more secure.
Most relevant here:

  • -mmitigate-rop Attempt to compile code without unintended return addresses, making ROP just a little harder.
  • -fstack-protector-all You need -fstack-protector-all to guarantee guards are applied to all functions, although this will likely incur a performance penalty. Consider -fstack-protector-strong as a middle ground. The -Wstack-protector flag here gives warnings for any functions that aren't going to get protected.
  • -­D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 Buffer overflow checks. See also difference between =2 and =1.
  • -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now RELRO (read-only relocation).
  • -Wl,-z,noexecstack Non-executable stack.

These options either give compiler warning (that you can make error), or a runtime error, preventing the damaged program to cause havoc.

Q: How to change app text or background color in Android Studio? A:

Using Jetpack Compose (Modern Kotlin) If you see @Composable functions in your MainActivity.kt, you are using Compose. You change colors directly in the Kotlin code.

Change Text Color -- Inside your Text component, use the color parameter:

Text(
    text = "Hello Android!",
    color = Color.Blue // Or Color(0xFF0000FF) for hex
)

Change Background Color -- Wrap your content in a Surface or a Box and set the color or background modifier:

Surface(
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize(),
    color = Color.White // Sets the background to white
) {
    Text(text = "Hello Android!", color = Color.Black)
}

Q: What is a good design for custom extensions to a Java class? A:

The subclass thing isn't really a subclass problem, it's this line:

extensions.put(extension.getClass(), extension);

You're deriving the key from the value. Everything else follows from that. The runtime class isn't necessarily the class the caller thinks they're storing, and once you've stored it you can't recover what they meant. Both other answers fix it by making the caller pass the key, and at that point there's nothing left to resolve, because you're not inferring anything.

I'd take Louis's Key<T> over Class<T>, for a reason that matters specifically to you as a library author rather than to a single application: Class is a shared namespace.

Two unrelated consumers of your library who both reach for String.class will silently clobber each other, and neither has any way of knowing the other exists. An identity-based Key is owned by whoever declares it, so that can't happen.
